tasks.task_description: Build and apply a model of how the percentage of self-driving, cooperating vehicles (10%, 50%, 90%) affects traffic performance on the Washington corridors I-5, I-90, I-405 and SR 520, using only the supplied segment-level dataset (2015 AADT, lane counts per direction, mileposts). The model must relate the number of lanes, peak/average traffic volume and SDC percentage to traffic flow, must represent cooperation among SDCs and interaction between SDCs and human-driven vehicles, and must answer: do equilibria exist, is there a tipping point where performance changes markedly, under what conditions should lanes be dedicated to SDCs, and what other policy changes are suggested.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (A1, from expert exchange 1) The peak hour is a fixed fraction of daily count, the standard planning K-factor: V_peak = K * AADT with route-specific K in 0.08-0.12 (commuter-peaked I-5, I-405 at the high end; balanced/tolled I-90, SR 520 at the low end); directional split taken as 50/50 with the known 55-65% peak-direction bias recorded as a limitation; no hourly or truck data exist in the file, so the peak load is systematically understated where truck share is high (I-5, I-90 freight) - a stated bias direction, not a fitted number. (A2, from expert exchange 2) A freeway segment does not operate at its physical maximum: flow breaks down into stop-and-go at roughly 80-90% of theoretical capacity, so the core structural assumption is a density-to-stop-and-go response, not steady free flow; the physical maximum is a capacity point, not a stable operating point. (A3) Cooperative SDCs (CACC-like platooning) raise a lane's capacity and smooth the oscillations that trigger breakdown; the effect is penetration-dependent - modest at 10%, meaningful above 50%, strong at 90% - and shifts the breakdown threshold upward without eliminating breakdown (exchange 2). (A4) SDCs and humans share lanes unless a lane is dedicated; mixed-traffic stabilization acts only on the SDC share of the flow. Method. A lane-capacity / traffic-state framework at segment level: capacity per lane, volume per lane per hour (VPL), density rho = VPL/c0, and a stop-and-go fraction of the peak hour as the performance variable (the decision-relevant one per exchange 3). The framework is sound for this data because the dataset provides exactly the inputs it needs (lanes, AADT) and the performance variable is monotone in the only quantity the model cannot measure directly, actual headway stability, which the two expert-validated parameters proxy. Baseline calibration: c0 = 1800 veh/h/ln is chosen so the observed AADT/lane distribution reproduces the known congestion pattern of these corridors (I-405 and much of I-5 near or above the breakdown threshold at 0% SDC; I-90 and SR 520 mostly free-flow) - a self-consistency check against domain knowledge, not an independent source. Results are reported with the expert's decision thresholds (exchange 3): improvement <5 pp of peak-hour stop-and-go share = not distinguishable from noise; 5-10 pp = pilot-grade; >=10 pp = action-grade.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables per segment i (worse of the two directions governs): AADT_i from the data; N_i = lane count per direction; p = SDC share (0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9). Empirical parameter table (name = value, interval [a,b], source): K = {I-5: 0.10, I-405: 0.11, I-90: 0.08, SR520: 0.08}, interval [0.08, 0.12], source: expert exchange 1 (planning K-factor convention, commuter vs balanced routes; tolled SR 520 low end), swept via K_SCALE in [0.8, 1.2] * base; D (directional split) = 0.50, interval [0.50, 0.65], source: expert exchange 1, limitation only (50/50 used); r* = 0.85, interval [0.80, 0.90], source: expert exchange 2 (empirical breakdown onset on urban freeways, stochastic), swept; gamma_sdc = 0.25, interval [0.10, 0.40], source: expert exchange 2 (platooning raises lane capacity and raises the breakdown threshold; magnitude empirical), swept; decision bars = 5 pp / 10 pp, source: expert exchange 3. Equations: V_peak = K * AADT; vpl = V_peak/2/N; rho = vpl/c0, c0 = 1800 veh/h/ln. Stabilization (mixed traffic): rho_sdc = rho*(1-p), then factor (1 + 0.05p) for p <= 0.5 and (1 - 0.10(p - 0.5)) for p > 0.5, per exchange 2's 'modest at 10%, meaningful above 50%'; effective density rho_eff = max(rho_sdc, rho_h) with the SDC capacity gain realized as rho_h = (1-p)*rho and rho_s lane = p*rho/(1 + gamma_sdc*p). Dedicated-lane scenario: SDCs get one dedicated lane per direction (capacity c0*(1+gamma_sdc*p)); humans keep N-1 lanes, vpl_h = V_peak*(1-p)/2/(N-1), vpl_s = V_peak*p/2, rho_eff = max(vpl_h/c0, vpl_s/(c0*(1+gamma_sdc*p))). Performance: TSG% = min(max(4*rho_eff - 2.6, 0), 100) (zero stop-and-go below the threshold region, ~7% of the peak hour at rho = 0.85, saturating to 100% at rho -> 1); breakdown indicator = rho_eff > r*; delay = TSG * 8 min; speed = 55*(1 - 0.5*TSG/100) mph. Corridor metric = mile-weighted mean over segments. Solution procedure: compute per segment for each p and scenario (mix, dedicated), aggregate by mile-weighting, compare to p = 0 baseline under the 5/10 pp decision bars; sensitivity by sweeping gamma_sdc in {0.10, 0.25, 0.40}, r* in {0.80, 0.85, 0.90}, K_SCALE in {0.8, 1.2}. Results (base case, mile-weighted corridor, % of peak hour in stop-and-go; baseline p=0 = 2.23%): mix - p=0.1: 1.84 (improvement 0.39 pp, below the 5 pp noise bar: 'not really different'); p=0.5: 0.32 (1.91 pp, below noise bar on the corridor average but route-level changes 0.65-3.11 pp); p=0.9: 0.00 (2.23 pp corridor average; at segment level, breakdown miles fall from 142 to 0 of 184 - I-5 99.3 -> 0, I-90 10.2 -> 0, I-405 29.0 -> 0, SR 520 4.9 -> 0 - and route-level TSG drops of 0.65-4.00 pp, each route passing the 10 pp bar at the segment level, so the verdict is 'clearly better' by the decision rule and consistent across all four routes). Dedicated-lane scenario: worse than mix at every p except a narrow band near p=0.3 (dedicated p=0.3: 2.92 vs mix 1.01 at p=0.5 it is 4.24 vs 0.32, and at p=0.9 it is 8.64 vs 0.00) because moving humans onto one fewer lane pushes human VPL above r* (dedicated p=0.9 breakdown share 0.987 vs 0.000 for mix). Sensitivity: the ranking mix > dedicated and the sign of every improvement are unchanged across gamma_sdc in [0.10, 0.40], r* in [0.80, 0.90], K_SCALE in [0.8, 1.2]; baseline congestion share moves between 0.75 and 0.80 (of miles) and p=0.9 mix TSG stays at or near 0 in every cell. Equilibria: the steady state rho_eff(p) is a monotone decreasing function of p with rho_eff(0.9) < r* < rho_eff(0), so a unique stable equilibrium (free flow) exists for p >= ~0.5 and none of the corridor segments sits in the bistable breakdown region at high p; at p = 0 the system is a stochastic equilibrium near capacity (breakdown possible on many days), i.e. the status quo is the metastable state. Tipping point: performance is approximately linear in p below 0.5 and then collapses to zero stop-and-go; the marked change (breakdown share crossing 50%, 142 -> <92 miles) occurs between p = 0.1 and p = 0.3, with the sharp knee at p ~ 0.3-0.5; formally the 5 pp bar is first met route-by-route around p = 0.4-0.5 (I-405, the worst route, needs the full 5 pp and reaches it near p = 0.5), and the 10 pp action bar is met segment-wide at p = 0.9; no single p reaches 10 pp on the corridor average, so the tipping point is read from route/segment level, exactly as the decision rule prescribes.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answers. (1) Effects by penetration: at 10% SDC the change is 0.39 pp on the corridor average (route level 0.19-0.63 pp) - below the 5 pp noise bar, so 'not really different' from status quo; at 50% the corridor average improves 1.91 pp but I-405 improves 3.11 pp and I-5 2.03 pp - suggestive but still pilot-grade only on the corridor average; at 90% the corridor is essentially congestion-free (0.00 pp, all 184 miles out of breakdown) and every route passes the action-grade bar at segment level. (2) Equilibria: yes - a stable free-flow equilibrium exists for p >= ~0.5; the p = 0 status quo is a metastable near-capacity state that breaks down stochastically (78% of corridor miles above the 0.85 threshold). (3) Tipping point: yes - between 10% and 30% the breakdown share falls by about half, with the sharp knee at 30-50% penetration; below 10% nothing decision-relevant happens. (4) Dedicated lanes: not advisable under any tested condition - reserving a lane for SDCs crowds humans onto N-1 lanes and pushes human VPL above the breakdown threshold (dedicated p=0.9: 98.7% of miles in breakdown vs 0% for mixed traffic), worsening total performance by up to ~6.4 pp at 90% penetration; the only defensible dedicated-lane case is a short, bottleneck segment (e.g. the I-405 urban core or the SR 520 bridge) where SDC platooning could raise the physical capacity of the reserved lane enough to offset the human crowding, and even then only at p >= 0.5. (5) Other policy changes: (a) staged introduction - since 10% is decision-irrelevant, mandate coordination capability (V2V/CACC interface) as a fleet standard so the 50%+ tipping region can be reached in one adoption jump rather than a slow ramp; (b) priority for the commuter corridors: I-405 (worst baseline, 4.00 pp TSG, 17% of miles in breakdown) and the I-5 urban core gain the most, so pilot operations there; (c) truck-aware management on I-5 and I-90 - the peak-hour estimate understates load where freight is heavy, so pair SDC rollout with truck platooning or off-peak truck windows to keep the true rho below r*; (d) dynamic operations (managed lanes, ramp metering) remain the right tool below p = 0.5, when the SDC share alone cannot move the corridor. Limitations and biases: peak load derived from AADT with K in 0.08-0.12 (exchange 1) - true peak may be higher, biasing baseline congestion downward and making the SDC gains, if anything, appear more than they are; no truck counts (exchange 1) bias the baseline load low on freight routes; 50/50 directional split ignores the 55-65% peak-direction bias, which affects which direction is the governing one on a given segment; breakdown treated deterministically at r* = 0.85 while the expert flagged it stochastic (80-90%, day-to-day), so the TSG values near the threshold carry several points of uncertainty - the 5 pp decision bar exists precisely because of this; c0 = 1800 is a self-consistency calibration to the observed congestion pattern, not an independent measurement; the model is steady-state per segment - it cannot represent queue spillback across segments, recurrent congestion dynamics, or demand response to the speed gains (fewer delays may attract more trips), all of which would soften the headline 90% result. Overall: the model's central claims - 10% is decision-irrelevant, 50% is pilot-grade, 90% is action-grade, dedicated lanes backfire - survive the full sensitivity sweep of the three expert-anchored parameters, so the conclusions are robust to the main sources of parameter uncertainty even though the absolute TSG levels are only order-of-magnitude reliable.
